title: The Mind at the Table
subtitle: Anchors, fairness, emotion and context in bargaining
summary: A narrated, interactive version of Lesson 3. It covers the same objectives — when to make the first offer and how to defend against an anchor, why fairness norms constrain agreements, and how to read the meta-analytic evidence on gender and negotiation — and leads into the same comprehension check.

visual.title: The mind at the table
visual.sub: Anchors, fairness, emotion and context in bargaining

cues.text: In the last two lectures, negotiators were calculators. They priced alternatives, found zones, traded across issues.
Real negotiators are not calculators. They get pulled by numbers, misread each other, and turn down money out of principle. This lecture is about those patterns, and how to design around them.
A hiring manager at a consulting firm asks a candidate for a senior data-science role: what are your salary expectations? This is a hypothetical example.
She has researched the market, but the range she found is wide.
If she names a number first, she may set the anchor the conversation revolves around. Or she may name a figure below what the firm budgeted, and never find out.
If she declines, the firm's number becomes the anchor. So, before we look at the evidence, commit to a view.

checkpoint.prompt: In a negotiation, does making the first offer help or hurt the person who makes it?

options.text: It always helps: the first number anchors the outcome.
It always hurts: you reveal information and lose flexibility.
It tends to help when the offerer is well informed about the zone, and can hurt when the offerer is not.

feedback.a: First offers do anchor, but an uninformed opening can be too generous, and then the anchor works against you.
feedback.b: The lab evidence points the other way: first offerers obtained better outcomes. The risk is specific to uninformed openings.
feedback.c: That is where the evidence and its limits lead. Informed first offers tend to anchor settlements in your favor; uninformed ones can give away surplus.
feedback.d: In Galinsky and Mussweiler’s experiments, first offers strongly predicted final prices. The effect is real; its size in the field is less certain.

items.label: buyer or seller: first offerer did better

cues.text: Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler ran three experiments on simulated price negotiations.
Whoever made the first offer, buyer or seller, obtained the better outcome.
First offers strongly predicted final settlement prices.
And this held both face to face and over e-mail.
The mechanism is anchoring. An anchor is a number present when you make an estimate that pulls the estimate toward itself. People start from it and adjust, but the adjustment usually stops too early.
In negotiation the anchor is rarely arbitrary. It is a deliberate claim, by someone who benefits from your adjusting too little.

cards.title: Their alternatives
cards.q: What will the offerer do without you?
cards.fail: Ignored, their number becomes your frame

cards.title: Their reservation price
cards.q: What is the least they would take?

cards.title: Your own target
cards.q: What did you come here to achieve?

cues.text: The same experiments tested defenses. The advantage disappeared when the recipient focused on information inconsistent with the offer.
The offerer's alternatives.
The offerer's reservation price.
Or the recipient's own target.
Notice what is not on that list: ignoring the number. That rarely works. The defense is to bring a competing reference point of your own.
So when the other side opens, do not reason from their number. Reason from your preparation, say so, and put your own number and its justification on the table.
Put together, the evidence supports a decision rule. Be clear: the rule is a practitioner heuristic built on the evidence, not something the experiments tested directly.
First, assess your information. Do you have reliable data on the zone: comparables, market rates, the other side's alternatives?
If you are informed, open first, ambitiously but defensibly, near or beyond your aspiration, with criteria attached.
If you are not, invite their offer or ask questions first. An uninformed opening can give away surplus.
And whoever opened, re-anchor: restate your analysis and counter promptly with your own justified number.
Back to our candidate. If her research really is weak, the honest answer to her dilemma is to learn more before she names a figure.

visual.sub: The fixed pie, and what it does to concessions.

cues.text: One more distortion, recalled from Lesson Two. Most negotiators enter talks expecting the other side's interests to be completely opposed to their own.

Thompson and Hastie argued that this misperception is a primary cause of inefficient agreements. The psychology reaches further: a negotiator who assumes opposition tends to discount the other side's concessions, and to read requests on compatible issues as hostile.

visual.title: The ultimatum game
steps: Proposer divides a sum of money
Responder accepts: both paid as proposed

cues.text: Now a game economists love, because it exposes a gap between theory and people.
In the ultimatum game, one player, the proposer, divides a sum of money.
The other, the responder, can accept, and both are paid as proposed.
Or reject, and both get nothing.
A purely self-interested responder should accept any positive amount. So a purely self-interested proposer should offer the smallest amount possible.
Across many published experiments, what share of the pie do you think proposers actually offer, on average?

checkpoint.prompt: Across published ultimatum-game experiments, what share of the pie did proposers offer on average?

feedback.correct: Right — about 40 percent, far above the “rational” minimum.
feedback.incorrect: The pooled average was about 40 percent of the pie — far above the minimum that pure self-interest predicts.

cues.text: Hessel Oosterbeek, Randolph Sloof and Gijs van de Kuilen pooled the evidence in a meta-analysis.
Seventy-five results.
From thirty-seven published papers.
Proposers offered, on average, about forty percent of the pie.
Responders' behavior varied across regions, and rejection rates fell when the pie was larger and when the share offered was larger.
The core finding: responders reject offers they regard as unfair, even though rejecting costs them money.

visual.sub: Objective criteria let the other side accept without appearing to lose.

cues.text: For negotiators, this means the other side's reservation value is not the only floor.
A counterpart who sees your offer as insulting may reject a deal that beats its alternative, especially when it can punish you at modest cost to itself.
Fairness norms, built from precedent, comparable deals and the history of the relationship, act as a second constraint beneath every agreement.
That is why objective criteria help. They turn a claim into a standard the other side can accept without appearing to lose.

A note on emotion, and a label: the lesson presents no specific study here, so treat this as practitioner heuristics. Visible frustration signals you are near your limit. Visible relief after a concession signals you would have paid more.
So name your own state before an important session, decide which reactions you are willing to show, and treat the other side's displays as data to interpret, not instructions to follow.

chapters.title: Who negotiates, and in what situation

cues.text: The third objective asks for discipline in reading evidence on a sensitive question: gender and negotiated outcomes.
A meta-analysis by Jens Mazei and colleagues pooled fifty-one studies.
Ten thousand eight hundred eighty-eight participants, from several countries, comparing the economic outcomes women and men obtain.

The difference favoring men was not fixed. Women did better when negotiating on behalf of another person, when they had information about the bargaining range, and when they had negotiation experience.
The pattern points to situations, more than stable traits, as the source of much of the gap. The authors emphasize that the difference can be lessened or even reversed.

lines: Which claim does the evidence support?

cues.text: Let's test how well you can read it.

checkpoint.prompt: Which claim is best supported by the Mazei meta-analysis?

options.text: The gap in negotiated outcomes depends on the situation, and clearer information about the range is associated with a smaller gap.
The lab effect size predicts the pay gap in a particular organization.
Because effects vary across studies, the evidence tells us nothing useful.

feedback.a: Not supported. The difference depended strongly on context and shrank or reversed in some conditions.
feedback.b: Right. Information about the bargaining range was one of the moderators; the pattern is context-dependent, which points to process levers.
feedback.c: Not supported. The studies were mostly simulations; effects do not transfer one-for-one to field settings.
feedback.d: Variation is the finding, not a reason to dismiss it: it identifies conditions under which the gap shrinks.

left.title: Over-claiming
points: An average difference is a fixed trait
Predicts how a given person negotiates

right.title: Under-claiming
points: Ignores the levers it points to

cues.text: The evidence demands that you resist two simplifications.
One reads an average difference as a fixed trait of individuals.
The other dismisses the evidence because effects vary. The meta-analysis supports neither.

And a methodological caution. A moderator analysis compares average effects across groups of studies. It pools thousands of participants, but it is correlational at the level of studies. The studies that used advocacy roles may differ in samples, tasks, years or countries.

Add that the evidence is mostly simulations, records gender as a binary category, and measures only economic outcomes. Enough to justify changing processes you control. Not enough to predict how any particular person will negotiate.

The practical response is to reduce ambiguity. Share ranges where policy allows, tell every candidate explicitly what is negotiable, and use the same structured conversation with each person. Those moves fit the moderators and ordinary fairness, and they assume nothing about any individual.

cards.title: Uninformed offer
cards.fail: Quick acceptance: you never learn their limit

cards.title: Extreme anchor
cards.q: Will they see it as absurd?

cards.title: Single-issue labs
cards.fail: One number has less room to work

cards.title: Magnitude
cards.q: How big in high-stakes field deals?

cues.text: Now the challenge. The first-offer advantage is real in the laboratory, but applied mechanically it produces four predictable mistakes.
It assumes the offer is informed. An uninformed opening can be too generous: they accept quickly and you never learn what they would have paid.
Extreme anchors carry costs the studies did not test. An absurd offer can end the conversation, exactly as the fairness evidence predicts.
Most evidence comes from single-issue price simulations. In multi-issue deals and repeated relationships, a single number has less room.
And anchoring in general holds up well, but the size of first-offer effects in high-stakes field negotiations is less well established.

The fairness evidence has limits too. Ultimatum responders cannot counteroffer, cannot walk to an alternative, and usually face a stranger once. The constraint survives the translation to real deals; the specific percentages do not.
Here is what the defense looks like in practice. A state agency is buying a case-management system. This is a hypothetical example.
The vendor proposes fourteen million dollars.
The agency's own estimate, built from three comparable implementations, is nine to ten million.
The weak response is to meet the vendor partway, at twelve million. That bargains from their number.

Instead the agency presents its estimate and the comparables, names its alternative, extending the current system with a smaller contractor, and asks the vendor to explain the difference line by line.

The conversation now revolves around two reference points, and one of them belongs to the agency. Then concede in decreasing steps, and explain each one, because unexplained concessions invite more pressure.

cues.text: Let's bring it together.
Informed first offers tend to anchor settlements; uninformed ones can give away surplus. Defend against an anchor by focusing on their alternatives, their reservation price, or your own target.

Offers perceived as unfair get rejected even at a cost, so justify claims with criteria. And outcomes depend on the situation as well as the person, which gives you process levers rather than stereotypes.
Most of this evidence comes from simulations: robust in direction, uncertain in field magnitude. Use it to design your preparation, not to predict a person.
Take the comprehension check below; it is the same as the written lesson's. Then use the Negotiation Chamber to practice opening and re-anchoring, and read Galinsky and Mussweiler's article itself.
The written lesson keeps the full tables and methodological notes. Thank you for working through this with me.
